result.summary: Io, driven to Egypt by a Fury sent by Juno, is restored to human shape when Jupiter swears by the Styx and Juno relents; she is worshipped as a goddess and bears Epaphus. Epaphus taunts Phaëton about his father, and Phaëton's mother Clymene swears he is the Sun's son, so he sets out for the Sun's rising.

scenes.title: Io's wanderings and restoration
scenes.summary: Juno sends a Fury to torment Io, who wanders to the Nile and begs Jupiter for relief. Juno is pacified and Io regains her human form and is worshipped.
scenes.stakes: Io risks endless torment and permanent loss of her human shape and voice.

scenes.title: Epaphus taunts Phaëton
scenes.summary: Io's son Epaphus is worshipped in Egypt. He mocks Phaëton for believing in an imaginary divine father, and Phaëton begs his mother for proof.
scenes.stakes: Phaëton's pride and standing, if his divine parentage cannot be proved.

scenes.title: Clymene's oath; Phaëton departs
scenes.summary: Clymene swears by the Sun that he is Phaëton's father and sends him to ask for himself. Phaëton eagerly sets off east past Ethiopia and India.
scenes.stakes: Clymene risks her sight if her oath is false; Phaëton seeks proof of his identity.

alias_notes.explanation: Phœbus is another name for the Sun god, Phaëton's father.
Io is worshipped in Egypt under the name Isis.
Jove is another name for Jupiter.

notable_quotes.reason: Epaphus's taunt sets off Phaëton's quest and the whole story that follows.

analysis.text: Divine anger and mercy pass from Io's story to Phaëton's, linking tales of parentage, proof and the cost of pride.
Ovid ties Io to the Egyptian goddess Isis, reflecting Greco-Roman habits of identifying foreign gods with their own myths.

fun_facts.text: Ovid's phrase 'linen-wearing throng' refers to Egyptian priests of Isis, who wore linen.

language_notes.text: "Argive mistress" means Io, who was a princess of Argos; Juno's rage is aimed at the rival Jupiter loved.
Swearing by the Stygian waters (the river Styx) was the gods' most binding oath, which even Jupiter could not break.
"Disposed of into five nails" means the hoof splits into the five fingers or toes of a human hand or foot.
Linen-wearing priests served Isis in Egypt; Io is identified with the goddess Isis.
"Grandson of Inachus" is Epaphus; Inachus was the river god of Argos and father of Io.
Merops is Clymene's husband, the mortal who passes as Phaëton's father. "Nuptial torches of his sisters" refers to their coming marriages.
"Reaches the skies in imagination" means he is so excited that he already pictures himself in heaven.

context_notes.text: The Nile marks the far edge of Io's wanderings; in the myth Egypt is where she is restored.
Phaëton's shame is the hinge of the story: his need for proof of his father leads to the disastrous chariot ride of the Sun.

literary_notes.text: The narrator turns to address the river Nile directly, giving the geographic endpoint a solemn, personal tone.
The piece-by-piece list of vanishing animal features makes the reversal of the transformation vivid and almost physical.
Clymene's doubled "thou, that thou" shows her passion and insistence as she swears the oath.
Phaëton's eager, unthinking haste toward the Sun hints at the recklessness that will bring his ruin.
